questions.question_text:
The travel times in minutes for four routes between Home ($H$) and School ($S$) are:
Route 1 ($H\text{–}A\text{–}S$): $15\text{ min}$
Route 2 ($H\text{–}B\text{–}S$): $18\text{ min}$
Route 3 ($H\text{–}A\text{–}B\text{–}S$): $13\text{ min}$
Route 4 ($H\text{–}C\text{–}S$): $16\text{ min}$
What is the shortest travel time from Home to School?

options.why: Assumed the path with fewer edges ($H\text{–}A\text{–}S$) is always faster.
Selected Route 4 without checking the lower time on Route 3.
Selected the longest travel time instead of the shortest.

questions.solution_text:
$H\text{–}A\text{–}S = 15\text{ min}$
$H\text{–}B\text{–}S = 18\text{ min}$
$H\text{–}A\text{–}B\text{–}S = 13\text{ min}$
$H\text{–}C\text{–}S = 16\text{ min}$
$\min(15, 18, 13, 16) = 13$
Shortest travel time: $13\text{ minutes}$ (via $H\text{–}A\text{–}B\text{–}S$)

questions.question_text:
Using Dijkstra's algorithm on a network from $S$ to $F$, the final vertex labels are:
$S(0), A(4), B(6), C(10), D(9), F(13)$.
The edge connecting $D$ and $F$ has weight $4$, and the edge connecting $C$ and $F$ has weight $5$.
What is the shortest path to $F$ and its length?

options.why: Added $10 + 5 = 15$ which is longer than the optimal label at $F$ ($13$).
Gave the label of vertex $D$ rather than destination vertex $F$.
Incorrectly claimed the path passed through $C$ since $10 + 5 \ne 13$.

questions.question_text: In Dijkstra's algorithm starting at vertex $S$, vertex $C$ has a direct edge $SC = 10$, but its recorded label is $8$. Which statement best explains why?

options.text: An indirect path from $S$ to $C$ via another vertex has a total weight of $8$, which is shorter than the direct edge
The algorithm subtracted $2$ because vertex $C$ is two edges away from the start
options.why: Dijkstra's algorithm never subtracts distance for edge counts.

options.text: The weight of the direct edge was discounted because $C$ has an even degree
options.why: Vertex degrees do not discount or alter edge weights in Dijkstra's algorithm.

options.text: The direct edge $SC$ was excluded because it forms a cycle in the graph
options.why: Dijkstra's algorithm operates on general graphs and does not drop edges due to cycles.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{Label}(C) = \min(10, 8)$
$= 8$
An indirect path from $S$ to $C$ has a lower cumulative weight of $8$ than the direct edge weight of $10$.

options.why: Chose path $A\to C\to D$ ($7 + 3 = 10$) which is longer than $A\to B\to C\to D$ ($9$).
Chose the direct branch $A\to B\to D$ ($4 + 9 = 13$) which is longer.
Miscalculated $4 + 2 + 3 = 11$ instead of $9$.

questions.solution_text:
$A\to B\to D = 4+9$
$=13$
$A\to C\to D = 7+3$
$=10$
$A\to B\to C\to D = 4+2+3$
$=9$
Shortest directed path: $A\to B\to C\to D$, weight: $9$

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the **shortest path** between two vertices and the **minimum spanning tree (MST)** of a connected weighted network?

options.text: The shortest path between two vertices does not necessarily lie inside the minimum spanning tree
The shortest path between any two vertices is always identical to the path between them in the MST
options.why: An MST minimises overall network wire/pipe length, not individual point-to-point path lengths.

options.text: An MST can only be constructed after all shortest paths have been computed with Dijkstra's algorithm
options.why: MST algorithms (such as Kruskal's or Prim's) do not require shortest path calculations.

options.text: The shortest path is always the path that uses the smallest number of edges
options.why: Shortest paths minimise total weight, which often uses more lower-weighted edges than a single heavy edge.

questions.solution_text:
An MST minimises the total sum of edge weights required to connect all vertices.
A shortest path minimises the weight between two specific endpoints and may include edges excluded from the MST.
The shortest path between two vertices does not necessarily lie inside the minimum spanning tree.
